sentence: Genital herpes is a sexually transmitted infection caused by the herpes simplex virus.
Genital herpes is a sexually transmitted infection caused by the herpes simplex virus (HSV).
One type of the virus is the same one that causes cold sores.
Most people who carry the virus do not notice any symptoms and do not know they have it.
When symptoms do appear, they clear up on their own but can come back.
There is no cure, but antiviral treatment and self-care can help.
note: NHS: no cure; antivirals help; cream/self-care options listed.

sentence: A doctor or nurse may be able to diagnose genital herpes by looking at symptoms such as blisters, sores and ulcers.
They will ask about the symptoms and may take a small swab from a blister or sore for testing.
There is no screening test for herpes in people without symptoms, so partners are only tested if they also have symptoms.
There is no cure for genital herpes, but treatment can help.
For a first episode, an antiviral medicine may be prescribed to stop symptoms getting worse, and the NHS says it needs to be started within 5 days of symptoms appearing.
Cream may be offered for the pain.
Recurrences often clear up without treatment, although antivirals can be used.
Some people who have frequent outbreaks may take antivirals long term.
Self-care includes keeping the area clean with plain or salt water and using a cold pack wrapped in a cloth.
Sex is best avoided until the sores have gone, because the virus is very easy to pass on from the first tingling or itching of an outbreak until the sores have fully healed.
Condoms lower the risk of passing the virus on, but not if they do not cover the infected area.
Sexual health services can advise on longer-term treatment that may also reduce the chance of passing the virus on to a partner.
For symptoms of genital herpes, the NHS advises going to a sexual health clinic as soon as possible; many offer a walk-in service.
A GP can also help but will probably refer to a sexual health clinic.
In pregnancy, a midwife or GP is the route if genital herpes is suspected.
note: NHS (via search summary): see midwife or GP if you think you have genital herpes in pregnancy.

sentence: For fever, headache or vomiting during or after an outbreak, MedlinePlus (US) advises contacting a healthcare provider, which in the UK would usually mean NHS 111 or a GP the same day.

sentence: For a medical emergency, call 999.
Genital herpes is an infection of the genital area caused by the herpes simplex virus.
The NHS says most people with the virus do not notice any symptoms, so many do not know they carry it.
Carrying the virus without symptoms is not a sign that anyone has done something wrong.
note: Neutral, non-blaming framing consistent with NHS text.

sentence: When symptoms do appear, they usually start between two and twelve days after contact with the virus, according to the NHS.
A first episode can bring spots or red bumps around the genital area and flu-like symptoms.
Blisters can burst to leave red, open sores around the genitals, anus, thighs or bottom.
note: Search summary blended NHS pages; attributed to the NHS page title returned.

sentence: A tingling, burning or itching feeling can signal that an episode is starting.
note: NHS-linked source in search summary mentions this.

sentence: Symptoms clear up on their own but can come back.
Repeat outbreaks are typically milder than the first.
Over time, outbreaks tend to happen less often and be less severe, and some people never have another outbreak.
Genital herpes is passed on mainly through sex, including vaginal, anal and oral sex.
note: NHS says passed on through sex; oral/anal/vaginal wording from an NHS Trust leaflet (Imperial) in same search.

sentence: The NHS says it can also pass on through skin contact with the infected area, even when no sores or blisters are visible.
It is very easy to pass on from the first tingling or itching of a new outbreak until the sores have fully healed.
One type of the virus is the same one that causes cold sores.
In the UK, BASHH describes HSV-1 as now the most common cause of genital herpes, while HSV-2 is more often linked to recurrent symptoms.
This means genital herpes is not always linked to a particular kind of partner or a particular kind of sex.
note: Plain deduction from HSV-1 being the commonest cause and the virus spreading by skin contact.

There is no screening test for people without symptoms, which is one reason the virus can spread without anyone knowing.

sentence: A doctor or nurse may be able to diagnose genital herpes by looking at symptoms such as blisters, sores and ulcers.
They will usually ask about the symptoms and may take a small swab from a blister or sore for testing.
The NHS says testing is free through sexual health services.
The NHS advises going to a sexual health clinic as soon as possible if symptoms appear.
A GP can also be seen, but will probably refer to a sexual health clinic.
Many sexual health clinics offer a walk-in service.
There is no screening test for herpes in people who have no symptoms.
Partners should only have a test if they also have symptoms.
The NHS says that a person who thinks they or a partner may have symptoms should get checked.
There is no cure for genital herpes, and treatment aims to ease symptoms and help outbreaks pass.
For a first episode, antiviral medicine may be prescribed to stop symptoms getting worse, and the NHS says it needs to be started within 5 days of symptoms appearing.
Cream may be offered for the pain.
Recurrences usually clear up without any treatment, although antivirals can be used.
For recurrences, antiviral medicine works best when started as soon as tingling, burning or itching begins, or as soon as blisters appear.
note: Search summary of NHS and clinic pages.

sentence: Some people with frequent outbreaks may take antivirals for a longer period.
US CDC guidance says that daily suppressive antiviral treatment reduces how often recurrences happen in people who have frequent recurrences.

The CDC adds that suppressive treatment is likely to reduce passing the virus on in people with a history of symptoms, and it should be combined with consistent condom use and avoiding sex during recurrences.
Self-care described by the NHS includes keeping the area clean with plain or salt water.
A cold pack wrapped in a cloth can ease the pain, and passing urine while pouring water over the genitals can help.
The NHS also advises avoiding tight clothing and avoiding touching sores unless applying cream.
The main concern in pregnancy is neonatal herpes, a serious illness in a newborn baby.
The NHS says there is a risk if a person has a herpes outbreak when giving birth, or gets genital herpes for the first time during pregnancy.
A person who has had genital herpes before pregnancy can usually expect a healthy pregnancy and a vaginal delivery.
The NHS says antiviral treatment may be offered from diagnosis until the birth if herpes is first caught after week 28 of pregnancy.
Other UK guidance describes different timings for antivirals, so the plan is made with the midwife or doctor.
note: NHS 111 Wales said week 36, UKHSA blog said around week 32; sources differ.

sentence: UK guidance from BASHH and the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists covers herpes in pregnancy and the newborn, with an update in 2024.
For a first episode late in pregnancy, UK guidance material suggests a planned caesarean may be advised, especially close to delivery.
note: BASHH algorithm per search summary: planned caesarean, especially within 6 weeks of delivery.

sentence: The NHS says to see a midwife or GP if genital herpes is suspected during pregnancy.
Symptoms often become milder and less frequent with time, according to the NHS.
Sex is best avoided until sores have gone, because the virus is very easy to pass on while sores are present.
Sexual health services can advise on longer-term treatment that may also reduce the chance of passing the virus on to a partner.
UK guidance from BASHH aims to limit both the physical and the psychological harm from genital herpes and to reduce passing the virus on.
This means a sexual health clinic can support emotional wellbeing as well as treat symptoms.

A sexual health clinic can talk through which options suit each person.
